stories.headline: Trump touts Venezuela oil deal, says it will drive down energy prices worldwide
stories.deck: US President Donald Trump announced a major oil deal with Venezuela. This agreement covers sixty-five billion barrels of oil and aims to lower global energy costs. The deal is expected to boost Venezuela's oil production significantly over time. Experts, however, believe immediate price changes are unlikely due to infrastructure needs. Trump also linked this policy to wider US interests in the…
stories.bodyText:
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said the oil deal between the United States and Venezuela will help drive down energy costs around the world, describing it as the "largest oil deal in history" and saying it covers 65 billion barrels of oil.
Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Trump said the agreement would benefit both Venezuela and the US, while adding that major global oil companies were entering Venezuela.
"The biggest oil companies in the world are going in [to Venezuela], and the numbers are absolutely incredible," Trump said.
Trump highlights 65 billion barrels of oil
Trump said the US and Venezuela had signed an agreement covering 65 billion barrels of oil, which he said would "benefit both Venezuela and the United States enormously and help drive down the cost of energy all over the world".
He also said the two countries together "have more than 60% of the oil in the world".
The deal centres on Venezuela's vast oil reserves and efforts to revive its oil industry.
Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez has said the agreement aims to increase the country's oil production to 1.5 million barrels per day.
The deal covers 17 oil fields with a proven potential of 65 billion barrels, according to Rodriguez's statement cited in the background copy.
It could bring $100 billion in investment into Venezuela's oil industry and generate more than $209 billion in taxes for Caracas.
Venezuela deal expected to boost oil production
The US government and an unnamed private operator in Venezuela have set up a new company with rights to untapped oil fields for 100 years, according to the background information.
The US is expected to receive 55% of the new company's effective output through an ownership stake and the right to buy oil at cost. A US official said oil bought by the US would go towards its strategic oil reserves and the military.
However, Venezuela's oil infrastructure is in poor condition and would require years and billions of dollars in investment to repair.
Trump has said the agreement will help lower gasoline prices in the US. But experts believe Venezuelan oil production was unlikely to increase quickly.
Amy Myers Jaffe of New York University said the deal could be helpful in the long run but would not immediately change retail gasoline prices. Kevin Book of ClearView Energy Partners said increasing production would take many years because of the scale of investment required.
Trump links Venezuela policy to wider US interests
Trump also highlighted the US military operation in January to arrest then-President Nicolás Maduro.
"Since that day, hundreds of Venezuelan political prisoners have been freed. They’ve let them out of jails, and we’re working closely with the leaders of Venezuela to forge a much better future for the Venezuelan people," Trump said.
"Our actions in Venezuela are proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere," he added.
The oil agreement has also faced criticism in Venezuela. Harvard University professor and former Venezuelan planning minister Ricardo Hausmann called it a "shameful deal", while criticising the agreement's legitimacy.
Trump expects Iran deal after US midterm election
In his UN remarks, Trump also said he believed the US would reach a deal with Iran after the November 3 midterm elections.
"I believe we'll make a deal right after the election because it doesn't make sense for them not to. They're waiting to see how I do in the midterm election," Trump said, according to Reuters.
Trump also raised the possibility of either reaching an agreement with Iran or taking military action, saying he had "a big decision to make".

stories.headline: Rs 1.79 lakh ITR, Rs 11.22 crore tax addition; ITAT gives chance if he plants 500 trees
stories.deck: The Assessing Officer examined the taxpayer's financial transactions and identified substantial cash deposits, unsecured loans running into crores and agricultural income of Rs 3 lakh that was not backed by supporting evidence.
stories.bodyText:
Your income tax return comes under scrutiny and you are given a chance to present your case before ITAT as part of your appeal you propose planting trees. A Haryana resident who reported an income of Rs 1,79,160 in his income tax return (ITR) for Assessment Year 2017-18, along with agricultural income of Rs 3 lakh, faced an income addition of Rs 11.22 crore after his return was selected for scrutiny.
The Income Tax Department issued statutory notices during the assessment proceedings, but according to the assessment order, the taxpayer did not provide the required information or supporting documents. The assessment consequently resulted in total income being determined at Rs 11,23,87,670 under Section 143(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961.
The taxpayer has now received what could be described as a rare opportunity to substantiate his case and contest the Rs 11.22 crore addition.
What the case is about
The Assessing Officer examined the taxpayer's financial transactions and identified substantial cash deposits, unsecured loans running into crores and agricultural income of Rs 3 lakh that was not backed by supporting evidence.
The assessment proceedings brought the following transactions to the tax officer's notice:
- Cash deposits of Rs 85.93 lakh in the taxpayer's bank accounts during the demonetisation period. The taxpayer was unable to explain the source of these deposits.
- Unsecured loans amounting to Rs 9,25,90,050.
- Sundry creditors of Rs 1,07,25,456. The taxpayer did not provide confirmations or other documentary evidence in support of these amounts.
The Assessing Officer consequently treated the amounts as unexplained credits or income, according to an ET report. 
These additions totalling Rs 11.22 crore were made to the taxpayer's income, taking his assessed total income to Rs 11.23 crore under Section 143(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961.
Karanjot Singh Khurana, Partner, DMD Advocates, told ET that the assessment order does not specify why the return was selected for scrutiny. However, he said the circumstances of the case themselves represented a typical trigger for scrutiny.
“It can be speculated that a return declaring Rs 1.79 lakh of income and Rs 3 lakh of agricultural income, against cash deposits of nearly Rs 86 lakh in the demonetisation window and a balance sheet carrying Rs 9.26 crore of unsecured loans could have been flagged in CASS for scrutiny assessment.”
What ITAT Chandigarh ruled
After the income additions were confirmed in the first appeal, the taxpayer approached the CIT(A), Gurgaon. His challenge before that authority did not succeed, following which he filed a further appeal before the ITAT Chandigarh.
This time, however, the taxpayer did not ask the tribunal to simply delete the entire income addition. Instead, he sought one final opportunity to place the necessary evidence before the Assessing Officer and substantiate his case.
His representative told the tribunal that the taxpayer was prepared to comply with any conditions that the Bench considered appropriate. As part of the proposal, he also offered to undertake the plantation of 500 trees as a measure of social and environmental responsibility.
The plantation was proposed to be carried out with the assistance of NGO Hari Yamuna Sehyog Samiti at the Yamuna Bank, Panipat, Samalakha Site.
The proposal covered the preparation of the land, labour expenses and the requirements for plantation. These activities could either be undertaken by the assessee himself or with the assistance of the NGO. In addition, he agreed to pay Rs 30 per plant per year towards maintenance for one year.
After examining the case details and considering the submissions made by both sides, the tribunal decided to give the taxpayer the final opportunity he had requested. The matter was sent back to the Assessing Officer, but only for the limited purpose of checking whether the condition imposed by the tribunal had been fulfilled.
Under the condition, the assessee has to plant 500 trees at the specified Yamuna Bank location within one month from the date of the tribunal's order. He is also responsible for ensuring their plantation, installation, protection and maintenance.
If the taxpayer chooses not to carry out the plantation himself, he has to deposit or pay the required amount for planting, installing, protecting and maintaining all 500 trees to the specified NGO within the same one-month period.
“It is, however, made absolutely clear that this relief is conditional,” ITAT Chandigarh said.
The tribunal further made it clear that failure to comply with the plantation requirement would result in the order of the CIT(A) being restored.
In other words, the tax dispute has not been finally settled at this stage. The unexplained money has also not yet been established or explained. The tribunal has simply provided the taxpayer with another opportunity to substantiate his explanation regarding the unexplained cash.
Why did the ITAT accept the assessee's willingness to plant 500 trees?
Karanjot Singh Khurana said three factors appear to have influenced the tribunal while considering the taxpayer's request.
The first was that the proposal to plant the trees appears to have originated with the taxpayer himself. The order indicates that the tribunal accepted an undertaking that had been voluntarily offered by the assessee.
Second, the Income Tax Department did not strongly oppose the proposal. Its submission was essentially that, if another opportunity was granted, the taxpayer should be required to comply with the conditions strictly and within a specified period.
The third factor was the evidentiary basis of the additions made by the lower authorities. The additions were based on the absence of supporting evidence before those authorities. Where important factual claims are sought to be supported before the tribunal for the first time through additional evidence, the tax tribunal would ordinarily consider sending the matter back to the lower authorities for examination.

briefs.headline: Samsung India profit falls 36% to 7,228 crore in FY26; mobile revenue declines
briefs.deck: In the Indian smartphone market, Samsung competes with Apple in the premium category, while facing intense competition from Chinese brands such as Vivo, Xiaomi, Oppo and Realme in the mass-market and affordable price segments
briefs.bodyText:
Samsung India Electronics profit declined 36% to ₹7,228.10 crore for the financial year ended March 31, 2026, according to a RoC filing by the consumer electronics major.
However, its revenue from operations rose slightly by 1.2% to ₹1.12 lakh crore in FY26, according to financial data accessed through the business intelligence platform Tofler.
Samsung India Electronics reported revenue from operations of ₹1,11,183.40 crore on a consolidated basis for FY25, and its profit stood at ₹11,287.50 crore.
Its total consolidated income, which includes other income, was ₹1,14,738.60 crore (1.14 lakh crore) in FY26.
An email sent to Samsung India Electronics seeking comments regarding the filing remained unanswered at the time of the story filing.
Part of the South Korean chaebol Samsung Electronics operates in segments such as mobile phones, tablets, televisions, home appliances and computers in the Indian market.
Samsung India Electronics gets its major contribution in the topline from the mobile phone business. In FY26, Samsung India's revenue from HHP (Hand Held Phones), including mobile phones and accessories, fell 1.35% to ₹81,472.2 crore. It was ₹82,595 crore in FY25.
In the Indian smartphone market, Samsung competes with Apple in the premium category, while facing intense competition from Chinese brands such as Vivo, Xiaomi, Oppo and Realme in the mass-market and affordable price segments.
However, revenue from the Home Appliances (HA) business, which covers its washing machines, air conditioners, refrigerators and microwave Ovens, increased 3.52% to ₹12,240.60 crore against ₹11,823.30 crore a year ago.
Its revenue from the audio-visual (AV) segment, which houses its TV and soundbar business, rose 8.5% to ₹8,055.90 crore in FY26 from ₹7,427 crore a year before.
Samsung is focusing on strengthening its television and appliances business, where it competes with players such as LG, Whirlpool, Haier and Voltas, as part of its strategy to diversify revenue streams beyond smartphones and benefit from growing demand for premium consumer durables.
Similarly, Samsung India Electronics' revenue from Software Development and Export (SDE) was also up 6.85% to ₹2,430.10 crore.
Samsung India Electronics is the only company in the Appliance & Consumer Electronics space with turnover above Rs 1 lakh crore.
India is one of Samsung's most important global markets, serving both as a large consumer base and a manufacturing hub for exports to several countries.
In FY26, Samsung's revenue from the domestic market was up 9.34% to ₹65,873.30 crore as against ₹60,243.50 crore a year before in FY25.
However, its total export revenue slipped 5.64% to ₹41,068.60 crore in FY26. It was ₹43,527.80 crore in FY25.
Samsung operates multiple research and development centres in India, including facilities in Bengaluru, Noida and Delhi-NCR, making the country one of its largest R&D bases outside South Korea.
Samsung India's total expenses inched up 3.54% to ₹1.04 lakh crore in FY26.
Its expenses of advertisement and promotion declined 11.9% to ₹3,850.50 crore in FY26 against ₹4,370.70 crore in the year-ago period.
Samsung India Electronics' 'cost royalty' paid to its South Korean parent entity climbed 7.2% to ₹3,474 crore from ₹3,240.50 crore in FY25. According to reports, this royalty is linked to the technical know-how, technology and manufacturing assistance provided by the parent for products manufactured in India, including smartphones, televisions, refrigerators, washing machines and air conditioners.

briefs.headline: ‘Squatting’ on mining assets a concern, says Mines Secretary
briefs.deck: Senior official says some miners do not commence operations within a stipulated time-frame, such ‘squatting’ rests on speculative tendencies
briefs.bodyText:
Certain miners holding on to their acquired blocks without commencing timely operations — or ‘squatting’ — is a cause for concern that the industry must look to address, Union Mines Secretary Keshav Chandra said at the 60th Annual General Meeting of the Federation of the Indian Mineral Industries (FIMI) here on Tuesday.
Separately, the senior official told mediapersons that India had kept prospects open on a return to lithium exploration in Mali. He also informed that a policy for processing of lithium and nickel was in the works.
Mr. Chandra mentioned that the government was also concerned about ‘squatting’ over mines.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the AGM, Mr. Chandra explained that mining commences after “arduous” process of approvals, including forest and environment clearances.
Thereafter, after the mining lease is signed, the miners are expected to commence operations within a given “substantial” time-frame. Despite that, some operations do not start, he said.
“It affects mineral wealth [of the country]; the production gets compromised. I requested members to expedite [operationalisation] and not contravene the provisions,” he said in response to a query from The Hindu.
In his address, Mr. Chandra said that ‘squatting’ would not help anybody and was centred on speculation.
“Squatting is not going to help anybody. It [squatting] is a speculation, so no activity should promote any speculation,” he said, emphasising the very purpose of government reforms in the mining sectors were aimed at accelerating production and ensure the country’s progress in this sector.
Mr. Chandra affirmed that India was looking “very openly” at visiting the Russian project for lithium extraction in Mali.
Russia’s State Atomic Energy Corporation had approached India last year for a collaborative effort for lithium extraction in the West African country.
It was reported that the pact was kept on hold owing to the political instability in Mali. “We are looking at it very openly. We are looking at all the possibilities,” he said in response to a query from The Hindu.
The Mines Secretary also said at the AGM that a “very substantial” scheme for domestic processing of nickel and lithium was in the works.
“For lithium and nickel, very soon we would be launching our [Mines Ministry’s] scheme,” he said, adding they would aid to localise the entire battery ecosystem relying on the two minerals.
Statutory clearances
In his address, outgoing president of the federation Shantesh Gureddi, highlighted that securing timely statutory clearances, notably forest clearances, entailed “lengthy” timelines and was “often hindered by procedural complexities”.
He added that the overall paradigm was further complicated with the involvement of multiple agencies, resulting in “overlapping jurisdictions, further complicating the process”.
“We humbly urge that these critical gaps be addressed expeditiously so that projects can proceed on time and the sector’s full potential can be realised,” he said.

briefs.headline: Steel prices at four-year high; trend to continue in H2: report
briefs.deck: The spike in prices is mainly due to rise in key raw materials coupled with an increase in demand, a BigMint analyst said
briefs.bodyText:
Domestic steel prices have touched a four-year high due to costlier raw materials, especially coking coal, coupled with rise in post monsoon demand, according to market research firm BigMint.
The trend is expected to continue over the remaining quarters of the ongoing fiscal year, it said in a report.
Hot rolled coil (HRC) and CRC — two of the most common types of flat steel products used globally — are trading at ₹64,000 per tonne and ₹75,000 a tonne, respectively. Such levels were last seen in June 2022, BigMint data showed.
From August 1, prices of HRC and CRC have increased by ₹6,000 per tonne and ₹8,500 a tonne, respectively. HRC and CRC were at ₹58,000/ tonne and ₹66,500/tonne at the start of August.
The spike in prices is mainly due to rise in key raw materials coupled with an increase in demand, a BigMint analyst said.
Coking coal, mainly imported, has seen a surge of around $65 per tonne to $305/tonne in just one month. While iron ore fines have seen a rise of ₹200-250 per tonne to ₹4,500 a tonne.
Coking coal alone contributes over 30% to the cost of steel production through blast furnace route.
In April-August FY27, the consumption of steel in India reached 70 MT, posting a 7% year-on-year rise.
On the outlook, BigMint said that the prices are unlikely to cool down in the remaining part of the fiscal as demand is expected to continue from both construction and infrastructure sector.
"These sectors consume 60 per cent of the steel produced in India and demand mostly comes after the post monsoon period every year," the analyst said adding the demand is also complemented from the automotive industry.
HRC and CRC are flat steel used in the auto, appliances and construction industries. Hence, any rise in the prices will impact the prices of vehicles, consumer goods and cost of construction as steel is a raw material for these sectors.

briefs.headline: RBI absorbs ₹71,971 crore liquidity from banks
briefs.deck: VRRR is the rate at which banks park their funds with the RBI. It is a tool that central banks use to suck liquidity
briefs.bodyText:
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has absorbed ₹71,971 crore liquidity from the banking system through overnight Variable Reverse Repo Rate (VRRR) auction, according to a notification released on Tuesday (September 22, 2026).
VRRR is the rate at which banks park their funds with the RBI. It is a tool that central banks use to suck liquidity.
The VRRR auction was held for ₹75,000 crore and offers were recieved for 96% of the amount for a rate of 5.24%. The overnight facility had a tenor of one day.
Keeping in mind that excess liquidity can be inflationary, the RBI has been absorbing excess liquidity from the system, especially after an overwhelming response from the special deposit scheme for NRIs filling up RBI’s coffers with $133 billion.
The VRRR operation also intends to bring the overnight call money rate in sync with the repo rate, ahead of a potential rate hike cycle.

briefs.headline: India-U.S. trade deal unlikely until competitor countries probed, tariffed
briefs.deck: An announcement of fresh 301 investigations against some of India’s competitor countries is likely soon, The Hindu has learned
briefs.bodyText:
India and the U.S. are unlikely to sign a trade deal until the U.S. launches a series of fresh ‘Section 301 investigations’, concludes them, and places tariffs on India’s competitors such as Pakistan, Sri Lanka and the Philippines, a person familiar with the process has said. It was a “strategic mistake”, according to the person, that Pakistan was not included in the list of countries probed in the excess capacity 301 investigations opened in March 2026.
100% U.S. tariff threat: Can India’s new trade deals reduce its dependence on America?
An announcement of fresh 301 investigations against some of India’s competitor countries is likely in the near future, The Hindu has learned, although the timelines and the subject matters for these 301s have not yet been decided. For this reason, it is highly unlikely that a trade deal will be concluded around Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal’s upcoming visit to the U.S. for the G20 trade ministerial that starts on September 30.
These developments appear to be consistent with Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal’s remarks at the Global Fintech Fest 2026 earlier this month. Mr. Agrawal had said that India operates largely on an MFN (Most Favoured Nation) tariff basis, while the U.S. operates on an executive tariff basis, and that a trade agreement would require an architecture with differentials and preferential market access structure for India.
The ‘301s’ are part of how the U.S. government is working around the February 2026 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that President Donald Trump’s ‘reciprocal’ tariffs were an unlawful application of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). Prior to this ruling, India and the U.S. had arrived at an Interim Agreement on trade that was announced via an India-U.S. joint statement issued on February 6.
Explained | Why has India-U.S. trade deal been delayed?
The general tariff rate for Indian goods entering the U.S. under the interim deal was going to be 18%, giving India an advantage over its main competitors. These include not just Pakistan (19%), which is the most politically sensitive country in New Delhi’s calculus, but also Vietnam (20%), Sri Lanka (20%), Bangladesh (19%) and the Philippines (19%). Nepal and the Maldives did not fall under the reciprocal tariff schedule and were tariffed at 10%. Following the scrapping of these tariffs, they trade with the U.S. on an MFN basis.
A central challenge to concluding the India-U.S. deal is that Pakistan, Sri Lanka and the Philippines were subject to 301 probes for forced labour, but are not on the 301 probe list for excess capacity, which India was subject to. Both probes were launched in March 2026. Pakistan, for instance, is tariffed at 10% as a result of the forced labour 301 investigation. So, at the moment, there are no similar legal instruments through which tariff rates on these countries could be raised further to their previous levels, while India is likely to be tariffed at 8% in the excess capacity investigation, bringing the overall tariff rate it faces back up to 18%.
To complicate matters, last Friday, Mr. Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law, enabling the executive branch of the U.S. government to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil. This includes India and China.
Also Read | Trade deal with India not far-off, but there are still gaps: U.S. official
The relationship between the existence of this new law and the likelihood that a bilateral trade deal will be signed is not straightforward. Sanctions can be suspended in the American national interest, as per the wording of the law. Additionally, the Trump administration is mindful of global oil prices and their link to the price of U.S. gas (petrol) at the pump, with the midterm elections scheduled for November 3. Global oil prices are impacted by India’s energy consumption and sourcing; New Delhi is the third-largest importer of crude oil globally and is the second-biggest market for Russian crude oil.
There is reporting to suggest that the bill, which was originally scheduled for consideration after the midterm elections, was rushed through in time for the September 24 meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and Mr. Trump in Washington, DC. China has reportedly been delaying the shipment of rare earths to U.S. and Japanese companies. U.S. officials had asked China to stick to recent commitments around export licences for rare earths, as per reporting from Reuters. This is one of the areas where the sanctioning authority could be used as leverage by the U.S. side in talks this week.
Another consideration is whether this new law increases the risk of Mr. Trump cancelling or substantially changing any draft U.S.-India deal (because his leverage has increased), as he has done in the context of other trading relationships.

briefs.headline: SEBI settles Hindenburg-related proceedings against Adani Group entities
briefs.deck: The proceedings related to the alleged non-disclosure of certain RPTs and instances where audit or limited review reports were signed by audit firms without holding a valid peer review certificate.
briefs.bodyText:
Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) settled adjudication proceedings against the five Adani group companies, for an amount of ₹1.5 crore, according to an order released September 22, 2026.
The proceedings relate to the now defunct short seller-researcher Hindenburg’s allegations regarding undisclosed related party transactions (RPTs) as well as violation of disclosure and corporate governance norms. Following this, the capital markets watchdog carried out an investigation into Hindenburg’s allegations of listing regulation and equity listing agreement violations.
In the investigation, SEBI found that Adani Enterprises Ltd. (AEL) said RPTs between Adani Estates Private Limited, a subsidiary of AEL and Vakoder Investment Ltd., a related party of AEL, were not disclosed in the Annual Report for FY2013. In addition to this, the company had violated other laws and rules under the Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirement,(LODR) and clauses in listing agreement.
The other four companies, Adani Total Gas Ltd., AWL Agri-Business Ltd. , Adani Green Energy Ltd. and Adani Energy Solutions Ltd. too were found violating LODR regulations, sections under SEBI Act and NSE, BSE bye laws.
ATGL, AABL, and AGEL violated LODR sections pertaining to non-peer-review of audit reports. AESL violated sections under the NSE and BSE Bye law in addition to clauses under its listing agreement.
SEBI sent a show cause notice to the five companies asking them to explain why an inquiry should not be held and penalties imposed for the alleged violations. Pending adjudication proceedings, the five companies proposed to settle with the regulator without admitting or denying the allegations.
Based on the settlement terms recommended by SEBI’s High Powered Advisory Committee, AEL paid ₹76.05 lakh, AGEL ₹45.50 lakh and the rest of the companies paid ₹9.75 lakh each.
“In view of the acceptance of the settlement terms and the receipt of settlement amount by SEBI, the instant adjudication proceedings initiated against the Applicants vide SCN dated February 15, 2024 is disposed of in terms of section 15JB of the SEBI Act and section 23JA of the SCRA read with regulation 23(1) of the Settlement Regulations on the basis of the settlement terms,” SEBI said in the settlement order.

briefs.headline: The China+1 question: Does India lose if Trump and Xi make peace?
briefs.bodyText:
Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington on September 23 for a three-day state visit. When US President Donald Trump welcomes Xi to the White House, the two leaders will have plenty to talk about: tariffs, artificial intelligence, rare earths, Taiwan and Iran.
India will not be on the agenda. But it will have plenty at stake.
Driving the news: From trade war to uneasy truce
US-China tensions have produced tariffs, technology restrictions and an accelerating effort by Western governments and companies to reduce their dependence on Chinese supply chains.
China has a stranglehold of rare earths and critical minerals. Xi demonstrated that he has a “Trump” card in US-China relations. When Beijing restricted exports amid its confrontation with Washington, the Trump admin had to make a retreat.
That leverage appears to have changed Washington's calculations. This is why the Trump administration has taken a less combative approach ahead of this summit, with analysts pointing to America's vulnerability to Chinese restrictions on critical minerals.
For now, both are trying to manage competition. And that distinction matters enormously to India.
Why it matters: India has been one of the beneficiaries of the great decoupling
The US-China rivalry has created many opportunities for India. 
Global companies began looking for a “China+1”. Supply-chain resilience became a national-security priority. The Quad acquired greater strategic relevance.
But even if Washington and Beijing find a sustainable way of doing business while continuing to compete, India's fundamental advantages remain. India is a large democracy, a potential manufacturing alternative to China, a technology power and an Indo-Pacific state capable of helping balance Beijing.
But what could change is the urgency with which others seek them.
Here are 5 Indian interests worth watching.
Zoom in: What happens to China+1 if China becomes less risky?
India's manufacturing opportunity has been one of the clearest dividends from US-China tensions.
The logic of China+1 was never that companies would abandon China altogether. It was that relying almost entirely on one manufacturing ecosystem had become too dangerous.
The operating logic changed from “just in time” to “just in case”.
India cashed on it. The PLI scheme sought to attract investment in electronics, telecom equipment, pharmaceuticals and other industries. Electronics production expanded. Apple's suppliers increased their Indian footprint.
US-China rivalry boosted India's mobile manufacturing, but a thaw could intensify competition
But consider what happens if US-China relations become more predictable.
China still possesses something India cannot replicate overnight: Gigantic supplier networks, world-class infrastructure, skilled labour, ports and manufacturing clusters built over decades.
If geopolitical risk falls, the premium companies are prepared to pay to manufacture elsewhere could fall with it.
That doesn't mean factories return to China. Covid alone taught global companies the value of diversification.
But the next factory location becomes a more competitive decision.
2. Chips and AI: What if the technology wall develops doors?
Semiconductors have become the defining battlefield of the US-China competition.
Washington has spent years restricting Chinese access to advanced chips and manufacturing technology. India, meanwhile, has positioned itself as a trusted technology partner.
The US-India TRUST initiative now encompasses semiconductors, AI, quantum technology, critical minerals, biotechnology, energy and space. It also envisages an AI infrastructure roadmap intended to accelerate US-origin AI investment and infrastructure in India.
But AI is also on the Trump-Xi agenda.
The two sides are exploring ways of managing risks from increasingly powerful AI models, although Washington remains committed to maintaining its technological advantage. China would also like relief from some US technology restrictions.
A summit will not dismantle America's technology controls.
However, if Washington permits more “non-sensitive” technology commerce with China, US companies regain access to an enormous market and Chinese firms gain additional room to operate.
India's proposition consequently has to evolve from “choose us because China is unavailable” to “choose us because India is indispensable.”
That's a much tougher test.
3. Rare earths: The minerals underneath the handshake
Rare earths may be the most important part of the summit that most people have never heard of.
They are essential to EV motors, wind turbines, electronics, chips and advanced weapons. And China dominates their processing.
That dependence gives Beijing an extraordinarily effective form of economic leverage.
It also creates an opening for India.
India and the US have already signed a Strategic Critical Minerals Cooperation Framework covering mining, processing, recycling, financing and resilient supply chains. India is separately developing rare-earth corridors in Odisha, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
But urgency is important.
China's critical-mineral dominance gives Beijing major leverage over global supply chains
The more insecure Washington feels about Chinese supplies, the stronger the incentive to finance alternatives.
If Trump secures predictable Chinese rare-earth exports, the immediate pressure to build expensive alternative supply chains could ease.
4. Russia and Iran: Watch what exemptions China gets
Then there is energy.
India and China are both major purchasers of energy from countries Washington wants to isolate.
The Trump administration wants Beijing to reduce purchases of Iranian oil, while US pressure over Russian energy has placed India in the firing line as well. Iran is expected to feature in the Trump-Xi discussions.
What if Beijing receives exemptions, tariff relief or other concessions as part of a wider bargain while India faces tougher treatment for pursuing its own energy interests?
India would be watching the energy fine print of any Trump-Xi agreement.
5. The Quad: Does India matter less when China looks less threatening?
The biggest question is strategic rather than economic.
The rise of the Quad - India, US, Japan and Australia - cannot be separated from anxiety about China's growing influence across the Indo-Pacific.
Yet a US-China detente does not make India's concerns about China disappear.
Beijing's relationship with Pakistan remains. Competition across the Indian Ocean remains. Taiwan and the South China Sea remain potential flashpoints.
And even amid the US-China thaw, Washington and New Delhi have continued building mechanisms explicitly intended to diversify critical-mineral and technology supply chains. The US-India critical-minerals framework signed this year is already in force.
So the Quad isn't about to disappear. But its political relevance could diminish.
India cannot outsource its rise to US-China rivalry
India should hardly wish for a US-China confrontation. A trade war between the world's two largest economies would damage the global growth.
India's advantages remain formidable: Scale, demographics, geography, technological talent, military weight and a huge domestic market.
But those advantages ultimately have to stand on their own.
India's task is to make sure its geopolitical value doesn't depend on how well or badly those two men get along.

stories.headline: How a Nagoya baseball ground was transformed into an Asian Games cricket venue
stories.deck: In Nagoya, a baseball field is poised for transformation into a cricket venue for the Asian Games. The Japan Cricket Association has generously invested in this endeavor, ensuring a top-notch facility for international teams. Notable hurdles involve creating high-quality cricket pitches using local materials. Once completed, the new turf wickets will serve men's tournaments before the ground…
stories.bodyText:
Nagoya: On the sidelines of the cricket facility at Korogi Athletic Park, a few Sri Lankan men sat watching the India-Sri Lanka women’s final. Not far away, an Australian kept a close eye on the proceedings.
They were not casual spectators. They were among the men who helped turn a baseball ground in a public park on the outskirts of Nagoya into a cricket venue capable of hosting the best teams in Asia.
Asian Games Full Coverage
 | 
Schedule
 | 
Medal Tally
The journey began in late September last year, when the decision was taken to include cricket in this edition of the 
Asian Games
. A little over 300 million yen was earmarked to create the infrastructure, including temporary stands with a capacity of 2,500 spectators.
Korogi was chosen because of the size of the facility. The Japan Cricket Association (JCA) also had a head start, having signed an MoU with Sri Lanka Cricket in March 2024, paving the way for Sri Lankan curators to be brought in.
At the centre of the operation was Jarrad Shearer, an Australian who has lived in Japan for the past 30 years.
“When it was decided that cricket would be part of the Asian Games, Alex Miyaji, the CEO of the JCA, approached me for a role because I had played some cricket back home in Perth and knew Japanese,” Shearer, a sports manager in the planning section of the organising committee, told TOI.
The transformation was no small job. The existing facility consisted of three baseball diamonds, with lines of trees demarcating the playing areas. The first task was to clear the trees and level the ground.
“We did the pitch and the outfield at the same time. While we were digging a hole to build the pitch, we were laying the outfield. So we created one hybrid wicket and four turf wickets,” said Shearer, who is also a Japanese translator by profession.
Gamini de Silva, former curator of Bangladesh’s Sher-e-Bangla National Stadium, and Asitha Wijesinghe, curator of Sri Lanka’s Pallekele International Stadium, came on board. They were joined by a few Sri Lankan-origin residents of Japan who had experience as groundsmen.
“While the four groundsmen are from here, Gamini and Asitha took turns to be here to oversee the preparations,” Shearer said.
Pitch construction, however, presented one of the biggest challenges.
“The pitch construction was interesting because we had a Japanese company doing it and they didn’t know anything about turf wickets. So our planning and instructions had to be spot on,” he said.
The pitches were built using layers of gravel, washed riverbed soil and 15cm of local Japanese clay.
“While we were testing the clay, we were informed that it was very similar to Pakistani clay,” Shearer said.
The surface got its first serious test in May during the T20 World Cup East Asia-Pacific Qualifier, when six matches were played on the hybrid wicket.
The plan was to use the turf wickets for the women’s competition, but heavy rain disrupted the schedule.
“The heavy rain a couple of weeks ago upset our plans and we couldn’t get the turf wickets ready in time. But we are confident that the men’s tournament will be held on those wickets,” Shearer said.
After October 3, when the men’s final is scheduled to be played, the facility will, in all probability, return to its original identity as a baseball ground for local children.
For now, though, the men who transformed it into an Asian Games cricket venue can stand on the sidelines and take pride in what they have created.

stories.headline: Japan gets a crash course in cricket as Asian Games bring sport to new audience
stories.deck: Cricket, although steeped in tradition in Japan, has yet to capture a massive fan base. With approximately 7,300 registered members in the Japan Cricket Association, awareness remains limited. To bridge this gap, Korogi Sports Park has introduced visual aids to enhance spectators' understanding. Meanwhile, Indian athletes struggle to find familiar dishes due to language barriers, but have managed…
stories.bodyText:
The first recorded cricket match in Japan was played 163 years ago in Yokohama, but the sport never quite caught the imagination of the Japanese. Currently, around 7,300 people are registered with the Japan Cricket Association – that’s about 0.00593% of the country’s population!
The tech-savvy nation, though, is leaving little to chance in its bid to create awareness about the game. At Korogi Sports Park, the venue for the cricket competition, spectators are handed a leaflet that breaks down the basics of the sport through easy-to-follow visuals.
Asian Games Full Coverage
 | 
Schedule
 | 
Medal Tally
It explains everything from the number of players on the field and fielding positions to umpires’ signals, the difference between a four and a six and how to read a scoreboard. Even the dimensions of the cricket field are put into perspective, with illustrations comparing them with football and baseball fields.
Hinata Sato, a baseball mum, arrived with her 10-year-old son Yuto to watch the women’s final on Tuesday. Having watched her son play baseball at the venue, curiosity brought them back to the makeshift cricket stadium.
“We have watched videos about cricket. My son wanted to watch it live and the ready reckoner helped him relate to what was happening on the ground. Cricket is really catching up in Japan,” she said.
Cuisine lost in translation
While the Indian men’s cricket team soaked in their first experience of Japanese cuisine by braving the rain in Tokyo to sample some local fare, athletes who have spent more than a week here are already craving for something familiar.
Those staying on cruise ships have access to Indian food, but athletes housed in hotels have been exploring Nagoya in search of restaurants serving a taste of home.
For one vegetarian athlete, the search was made more difficult by the language barrier and unfamiliarity with Japanese cuisine.
“Hum ghaas-phoos khane wale ka struggle bahut hai! Most restaurants have a non-veg odour that doesn’t agree with me. Language is a huge problem. When you ask for food without meat, they don’t understand,” the athlete said.
“I’m super glad to have found a couple of Indian restaurants. They have been very warm, gave us their contact details and sent us food whenever we asked.”

stories.headline: Steve Smith returns to South Africa: Between the deed and the redemption falls the shadow
stories.deck: Smith, who is a modern great, but this focus on what his action did to him rather than to his team or the game throws light on the gap between self-obsession and self-awareness
stories.bodyText:
So Steve Smith was ‘traumatised’ at the reaction to his act of cheating in a Test match. Australia are in South Africa for their first Test series after the incident known as ‘sandpapergate’. On their last tour in 2018 Smith was captain and had a role in using sandpaper to tamper with the ball in violation of the laws of the game.
Smith’s vice-captain David Warner was banned too; there has been an interesting narrative since. When Smith returned to the crease post-ban, he made 144 and 142 in the Edgbaston Test despite relentless booing and hostility from the English crowd. He finished with 774 runs in the series, a tale of guts and gumption. Was it the start or the end of redemption?
In the same series, Warner made 95 in 10 innings, being dismissed seven times by Stuart Broad. But he later made an unbeaten 335, the highest score by an Australian against Pakistan. According to Geoff Lemon, who wrote a book on the sandpaper story, “Public opinion firmly settled on Warner being the criminal and Smith the innocent bystander.”
Smith, who has the best average among players with over 10,000 Test runs (and for long averaged over 60, second only to Don Bradman), is a modern great, but this focus on what his action did to him rather than to his team or the game throws light on the gap between self-obsession and self-awareness.
As cricket writer Gideon Haigh told a television channel, “What is extraordinary is how it was done and how easily it was agreed to by the team and how, not unapologetic, but sort of oblivious to the consequences Smith and Cameron Bancroft seemed to be at the press conference.”
That mindset was of a piece with the one that led to the act in the first place, the entitlement and ‘win-at-all-costs’ philosophy encouraged by the cricket board for whom winning led to greater public interest which led to higher sponsorships. Everything was forgiven till it led to an act that could not be forgiven.
“I was thrown to the wolves,” complained Smith at the same press conference where he hoped to garner sympathy for the personal trauma. There’s something ingenuous in that admission coming from one who had asked a youngster, Bancroft, to do the dirty deed in the hope of avoiding responsibility.
It is not difficult to understand how a cricketer as obsessed with batting (and winning) as Smith can become more human through suffering. And every person deserves a second chance, especially if a debt arising out of an illicit act has been paid. Initially this column had asked for a life ban.
And then it struck me that cricket is only a game, an artificial construct whatever the qualities we breathe into it. And no matter if we feel it represents all the best society has to offer. The artificiality means we can impose upon it rules of behaviour that are ideal even if unattainable in the world outside.
Sport is morally neutral, although the acts of athletes may not be so. That cricket had to tag on a ‘spirit of cricket’ as preamble to the laws is indication that unwritten rules — the pride (and essence) of the game — was being taken advantage of consistently. That says more about the players and the times we live in than the game.
Many international cricketers felt that the bans were cruel, and the so-called ‘Australian way’ had to shoulder some of the blame. Trevor Chappell, pilloried for bowling under-arm to a New Zealand batter to prevent him from scoring the winning runs, had this to say: “(Smith and the others) will struggle for the rest of their lives. I haven’t been able to shake off what happened to me in 37 years. I come up on Google as the man who took the lead role in Australian cricket’s darkest day. It’s a relief I can finally drop that title.” Who will relieve Smith and Warner, apparently the current title holders?
Smith’s reception in South Africa when he returned for a white-ball tour was relatively mild. Still, he knows that crowds everywhere have a ready jeer, a reminder of trauma, at hand. And that has been his real punishment.

briefs.headline: Roshibina Devi assures medal after second chance, one win away from Asian Games final
briefs.deck: Naorem Roshibina Devi was initially not selected for the Asian Games but received a late opportunity. After Divyanshi Choudhary was injured, Roshibina took her place in the team. She has performed well, securing at least a bronze medal after defeating her opponents. This achievement follows her previous successes in Jakarta and Hangzhou, where she earned a bronze and a silver medal. Roshibina…
briefs.bodyText:
New Delhi:
 She wasn't supposed to be in Aich-Nagoya. Not at the Asian Games. Not at her third successive continental event. And certainly not one win away from a place in the women's 60kg sanda final.
Naorem Roshibina Devi had lost fairly in the selection trials for the Games, held in Srinagar in June. Her teammate Divyanshi Choudhary beat her in the semifinals and went on to win the trials, earning the original berth in India's wushu squad.
Asian Games Full Coverage
| 
Schedule
| 
Medal Tally
Roshibina had accepted her fate. After winning bronze at Jakarta 2018 and silver at Hangzhou 2023, she appeared set to miss her third continental Games.
Then came a sudden twist of fate.
Divyanshi was subsequently ruled out after the Wushu Association of India (WAI) said an MRI showed a high-grade ACL tear with large effusion. The federation replaced her with Roshibina, reopening a door the Manipuri had thought was firmly shut.
And she has made the most of it.
On Tuesday, Roshibina defeated Macau's Chu Man Sin 5-0 in the women's 60kg sanda quarterfinal at the Aichi Prefectural Martial Arts Hall to storm into the semifinals and assure herself of at least a bronze medal. 
A day earlier, she had beaten Bangladesh's Shika Khatun in the pre-quarters.
Now she has a chance to go one step further — and change the colour of her medal.
The 25-year-old has already changed colours once at the Asian Games. After her bronze in Jakarta, she ended India's 13-year wait for a wushu silver at Hangzhou, finishing second in the same 60kg sanda event.
Now, another medal is assured, gold is her target.
Her return to the squad, however, came amid a controversy. Divyanshi, who had beaten Roshibina in the trials, disputed her replacement and alleged harassment, while the federation rejected the allegations and maintained that the decision was solely medical.
In other matches involving Indians, Hanjabam Langlentombi Devi finished ninth in women’s Nanquan & Nandao, while Aryan Thakur lost 1-2 to Uzbekistan’s Saydullo Aburashitov in the men’s 56kg sanda quarterfinal.

briefs.headline: Pranati Nayak qualifies for Asian Games vault final, sets up shot at redemption
briefs.deck: Pranati Nayak has officially qualified for the vault final at the Asian Games, scoring an impressive 12.916. Her routine featured a challenging Tsukahara back 360-degree turn and a handspring pike forward somersault. Coach Ashok Mishra set this benchmark ahead of the event, and now Pranati looks forward to Thursday's final to improve upon her last outing at the Commonwealth Games.
briefs.bodyText:
After a disappointing show at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Pranati Nayak gave herself a chance to make amends by qualifying for the vault final at the Asian Games on Tuesday.
The 31-year-old, India’s lone artistic gymnast at the continental meet, finished seventh in the qualification round at Nagoya General Gymnasium with an aggregate score of 12.916 that also included a bonus of 0.20.
In her first vault — a Tsukahara back 360-degree turn with straight body — which had a difficulty value of 4.4, Pranati earned 8.600 for execution to score 13.000. She followed it up with a 4.0-difficulty vault — handspring pike forward somersault with half turn — scoring 8.433 for execution earning a total of 12.433.
It was enough to scrape through to the final, which will also feature Uzbekistan’s 51-year-old Oksana Chusovitina after she qualified in fourth spot with an aggregate score of 13.266.
The two-time Olympic medallist, who missed the 2006 and 2010 Asian Games while representing Germany, is competing in her seventh edition of the continental meet. When Chusovitina made her Asian Games debut in Hiroshima in 1994, several members of the 2026 field were not yet born.
For Pranati’s coach Ashok Mishra, however, the result was significant for a simpler reason: she had achieved the target he had set before the competition.
“It’s going to be a very difficult test for her. But I think she will do well,” Mishra had told 
TOI before the Games.
Considering she was struggling with plantar fasciitis, much of Pranati's recent training had also been about getting comfortable with the physical and psychological demands of the landing, with Mishra using soft-landing equipment and the foam pit before shifting her to the main landing area.
Pranati, however, showed no signs of discomfort on Tuesday as she secured place in the final, although there was little separating her from the gymnasts immediately below her.
As for South Korea’s Seojeong Yeo, she led the field with a score of 14.466 to qualify comfortably for the final. North Korea’s Chang Ok An was second on 13.900, while China’s DU Siyu secured the third qualifying spot with 13.433.
For Pranati, who trains at Odisha AM/NS India Gymnastics High-Performance Centre in Bhubaneswar, the qualification provides an opportunity to put behind the disappointment of Glasgow, where a lack of speed in her approach disrupted her first vault and kept her out of the final.
She will now return to the runway on Thursday with the chance to improve on Tuesday’s performance when the medals are decided.

briefs.headline: Asian Games Day 4: Bhaker targets 10m air pistol qualification, Chanu in action soon
briefs.bodyText:
In the women’s 10m air pistol qualification, India completes three of the six series. Manu Bhaker shoots a strong 97 in her third series, now finding fifth place overall.
Suruchi Inder Singh also records 97, climbing to 23rd, while Esha Singh currently sits 34th. With three series still remaining, the Indian shooters have time to improve their positions and push towards qualification for the individual final.
In the men’s pair heats, Jaswinder Singh and Nitin Kumar finish fourth and last with a time of 6:36.90, around 16 seconds behind the leader.
They qualify for Final B, which does not offer a medal opportunity. In women’s canoe single 200m, Megha Pradeep finishes fifth in 49.675, trailing the leader by about 2.733 seconds.
The result is not enough to reach Final A, but she advances to the semifinal, keeping her competition alive.
Manu Bhaker produces a strong third series of 98, moving up to sixth place in the women’s 10m air pistol qualification and boosting India’s hopes. Suruchi Inder Singh scores 94 in her second series, while Esha Singh records 93, leaving both outside the top 30 for now.
Meanwhile, in table tennis mixed doubles, Harmeet Desai and Yashaswini Ghorpade recover well after losing the opening game to Maldives. The Indian pair wins the next two games 11-6 and 11-7, turning the match around and taking a 2-1 lead.
India faces a mixed start across table tennis and shooting. In table tennis mixed doubles Round 2, Harmeet Desai and Yashaswini Ghorpade drop the opening game against Maldives’ Mohamed Ismail and Fathimath Ali.
Meanwhile, in women’s 10m air pistol qualification, Manu Bhaker scores 96 in her second series, while Suruchi Inder Singh and Esha Singh also struggle to make a strong start.
Based on the current averages, Manu sits 15th, with Suruchi 36th and Esha 37th, leaving all three needing improved scores in the remaining series.
India’s Harshwardhan Shaktawat, Varinder Singh, L Naocha Singh Oinam and Arun Singh secure a place in the final of the men’s kayak four 500m after finishing third in Heat 1.
The Indian quartet clocks 1:29.447, finishing 5.594 seconds behind leaders China.
Despite the significant gap to the front, their third-place finish is enough to advance to the final. India now has another opportunity to challenge for a medal in the event, with the quartet set to return for the decisive race.
India’s rowing campaign is showing encouraging progress. Balraj Panwar finishes third in his Men’s Singles Sculls heat in 6:52.84 and places fourth overall across the two heats, earning a spot in the Final A. He is only 0.31 seconds off a medal position.
In the Men’s Double Sculls, Satnam Singh and Salman Khan also finish second in their heat and fourth overall, securing their place in tomorrow’s final.
Earlier in the race, the pair holds second at the halfway point, three seconds behind China. Meanwhile, India’s men’s sepaktakraw team faces the Philippines in their final Group B match.
India will have another busy day at the Asian Games 2026 on Wednesday, September 23, with several of the country's top athletes in action in Aichi-Nagoya. Shooting and weightlifting will lead India's medal hopes on Day 4, while the men's badminton team will play for a place in the gold medal match.
Double Olympic medallist Manu Bhaker will be one of the main attractions of the day. She will compete in the women's 10m air pistol qualification alongside Suruchi Inder Singh and Esha Singh. The trio will also take part in the team event, and Bhaker, Suruchi and Esha will compete in the individual final if they qualify.
India's continental dominance in women's cricket remained unchallenged as the side delivered the country's first gold medal of the ongoing Asian Games, while the men's badminton team produced a stunning performance against Japan to assure itself of a podium finish on an eventful Tuesday in Aichi-Nagoya. Harmanpreet Kaur and Co. hammered Sri Lanka by 147 runs in the women's cricket final to successfully defend their Asian Games title, taking India's medal tally to seven and finally adding the much-awaited gold to the country's haul.
India also assured themselves medals in men's badminton and wushu, while the men's hockey side continued its goal-scoring spree with another emphatic victory, crushing Sri Lanka 16-1 in a Pool A encounter. There were contrasting fortunes in shooting and table tennis, while India's boxers continued their unbeaten run and gymnast Pranati Nayak qualified for the vault final.
Hello, and welcome to live coverage of the Asian Games 2026 Day 4.
India’s campaign at the 20th Asian Games, Aichi-Nagoya 2026, continues on Wednesday, with athletes competing across several sports.
India will compete in shooting, swimming, hockey, badminton, table tennis, and many other events. There will also be medal opportunities for the Indian contingent.

briefs.headline: La Liga president hits out at Real Madrid refereeing ‘conspiracy’ claims
briefs.deck: Here they go again, the mouthpieces and the regime’s television, building the same old narrative — the permanent conspiracy, said La Liga president Javier Tebas
briefs.bodyText:
La Liga president Javier Tebas hit out on Tuesday (September 22, 2026) at what he deemed accusations of a refereeing "conspiracy" by Real Madrid following their derby loss to Atletico Madrid.
Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho brought two printed screenshots of what he thought were red-card tackles committed by Atletico players to his post-match press conference following Sunday's (September 20) 2-1 defeat.
Tebas responded to a pro-Real article on social media with a lengthy riposte to allegations of a "conspiracy" against the 15-time European champions.
"Here they go again, the mouthpieces and the regime's television, building the same old narrative — the permanent conspiracy," said Tebas, who has often been at odds with Real Madrid and the club's outspoken president Florentino Perez.
"This article goes further — it claims that referees harm 'The business that feeds them'.
"What exactly is it asking for? Refereeing based on revenue, viewership, or the badge? What a way to understand equality in the competition.
"Real Madrid are crucial to La Liga. But claiming that 'La Liga is worth nothing' without them reveals the disdain for the other clubs, their fans, and their history. The competition belongs to no one."
Madrid have made a stuttering start to the season and already sit six points behind champions and early leaders Barcelona in the La Liga table.
"Claiming that referees are directed against Real Madrid is living in another galaxy," added Tebas.
"That narrative serves as an excuse to cover up other shortcomings that are plain to see in these first matches of the season.
"It's more comfortable to point to a conspiracy than to explain what's happening on the pitch."
Madrid responded to Tebas's comments later Tuesday (September 22), calling them "intolerable".
"Our club considers it intolerable that the president of La Liga uses his institutional position to continue discrediting and attacking Real Madrid in the manner he does in each of his public interventions," the club said in a statement.
"Given this inappropriate behavior, which has persisted over time, we believe that professional football in Spain urgently needs a leader capable of managing it and developing its full potential with the fundamental duty of neutrality."
Mourinho returned for a second spell in charge at the Santiago Bernabéu in the close-season, tasked with ending a two-year spell without a major trophy.
On Tuesday (September 22), the technical committee of referees acknowledged "a clear and obvious error" regarding one of the fouls cited by Mourinho, adding that VAR should have intervened.

briefs.headline: CSK's Vansh Bedi says he is not the unnamed player in sting operation row
briefs.deck: Bedi, who was part of the Chennai Super Kings (CSK) set-up during IPL 2025 and later played for Central Delhi Kings in the Delhi Premier League (DPL), broke his silence.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Delhi wicketkeeper-batter Vansh Bedi has denied any connection with the controversy surrounding a sting operation that alleged the misuse of confidential team information in Indian cricket, saying attempts to link him to the case are "false and defamatory".
Bedi, who was part of the 
Chennai Super Kings
 (CSK) set-up during IPL 2025 and later played for Central Delhi Kings in the Delhi Premier League (DPL), broke his silence on Tuesday after his name began circulating on social media following an undercover investigation involving former domestic cricketer Rachit Bhatia.
In a statement posted on Instagram, Bedi said he was not the unnamed CSK player mentioned during the sting operation and had no involvement in the allegations made by Bhatia.
“I categorically state that I am not the individual referred to by Ex-Ranji Trophy cricketer Rachit Bhatia in the sting operation concerning alleged match-fixing involving a CSK player, nor do I have any involvement whatsoever in any such activity,” Bedi wrote.
He also said that any attempt to connect him with the allegations was defamatory and that his legal team had started the process of taking action.
Bedi said his lawyers were pursuing “appropriate civil and criminal action” against those responsible for circulating the claims.
The original undercover investigation did not identify Bedi as the player who allegedly supplied confidential information to Bhatia. However, his name later began circulating online.
Earlier on Tuesday, the Delhi & District Cricket Association (DDCA) also responded to media reports about alleged corruption in the Delhi Premier League, calling the allegations "unverified".
“DDCA would like to clarify that the allegations referred to in these reports are unverified and have not been established by any competent authority. The Association believes it would be inappropriate to draw conclusions about any individual, player or franchise based solely on such allegations,” the DDCA said in a statement.
“Given the seriousness of the matter, DDCA has written to the respective authorities and shared the information that has come to its notice, requesting that the matter be examined through the appropriate established processes.”

briefs.headline: Brazil Legends and Indian All Stars to rekindle football magic
briefs.bodyText:
Memories will visit the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium on Wednesday night.
Memories of Ronaldinho and Rivaldo from the World Cup. Of I.M. Vijayan and Jo Paul Ancheri scoring some great goals at the Indian football ground.
The match between Brazil Legends and Indian All Stars could indeed make the football fans nostalgic.
The game, organised by Gammen Sports & Entertainment, is the second act of the return of the Titan series, according to the organisers. In the first, played in Chennai last year, Brazil had won 2-1.
The fans would be hoping to see a few goals in the return leg, too. They may not mind some moments of magic from Ronaldinho and Rivaldo, in particular.
The Brazilian side also includes Edmilson, Paulo Sergio, Giovanni, Roque Junior, Viola, Gomes, Amaral, Gustavo Nery, Ricardo Oliveira, Jorginho, Camanducaia, Elivelton, Souza, Para and Diogo.
The Indian line-up features Bhaichung Bhutia, C.K. Vineeth, Mohammed Rafi, Climax Lawrence, M.V. Nelson, Gouramangi Singh, Arnab Mandal, Mahesh Gawli, Mehrajuddin Wadoo and Mehtab Hossain.
The match kicks off at 7.30 p.m.

briefs.headline: TNPL was a new experience as the crowd was different, says Vineeth
briefs.bodyText:
V.K. Vineeth didn’t feature in Tamil Nadu’s under-14 or under-16 teams.
But he made the Vinoo Mankad and Cooch Behar Trophy squads and, last season, emerged as the Vinoo Mankad Trophy’s top run-scorer with 488 runs.
Then came the High Performance Camp at CoE, followed by a tour of Sri Lanka with India u-19, where he scored a hundred in a youth ODI.
Vineeth is part of India u-19’s series against Australia. On Monday, he scored a gritty 87 as India sealed the series.
His story began in Chennai, where he started playing cricket at seven. His father, a Southern Railway RPF employee, introduced him to the game. His elder brother, K. Veeraviswa, who played Tamil Nadu u-19, became another influence.
The TNPL, however, gave him his first taste of a crowd. “When I went on to play the TNPL for the Dindigul Dragons this year, it was a whole new experience because the crowd was different. So playing in front of a crowd and under the lights for the first time was unbelievable,” Vineeth told The Hindu.
He initially carried water, but mentor R. Ashwin, B. Indrajith and Sandeep Warrier helped him settle. “They said whether the crowd comes or not, we are going to play cricket. That is our main part. The crowd is just an add-on.”
Vineeth featured in three games for the Dindigul Dragons, scoring 82 runs.
A Virat Kohli fan, Vineeth has learnt to live with missed milestones. “I don’t try to hide my mistakes. I try to understand what I have to improve and what I can take from the learnings,” the 18-year-old said.
Away from cricket, he listens to songs and writes a diary. “The game is over, the day is over,” he said, adding: “The next day, we have to start afresh.”
Match starts at 9 a.m.
